chunks: What is sampling?. The question: What is sampling?
Sampling means recording a signal's value only at evenly spaced instants, so a smooth curve becomes a list of numbers.
If you sample more than twice as fast as the fastest frequency in the signal, no information is lost. If you sample too slowly, fast changes get mistaken for slow ones.
That mistake is called aliasing.
A movie camera takes a fixed number of frames per second.
When a wagon wheel spins quickly, the wheel can look like it turns slowly or even backwards, because each frame catches it at a slightly different spot.
The camera did not see the real motion, only snapshots. A sampler works the same way.
The difference is that a sampler records numbers, not pictures, and cannot undo the mistake afterward.
Eight samples per cycle land on the sine and clearly trace it out.
The sample points are all you'd keep, but the smooth curve through them is the only band-limited signal that fits, which is what the reconstruction filter finds.
Sample rate: how many samples are taken per second. Nyquist rate: ("Nyquist rate and why it matters"): twice the highest frequency in the signal. You must sample faster than this.
Aliasing: a frequency that is too high showing up in the samples as a lower, false one.
Anti-alias filter: a filter placed before the sampler that removes frequencies that are too high to sample correctly.
Quantization: rounding each sample to one of a fixed set of levels. Sampling cuts up time, and quantization cuts up amplitude.
Sample at 1,000 samples per second. A 100 hertz tone gets 10 samples per cycle, which is plenty. A 900 hertz tone is above half the sample rate (500 hertz), so it aliases.
The samples are exactly the ones a 1,000 minus 900 = 100 hertz tone would give, so the 900 hertz tone looks like 100 hertz. That is why you filter before sampling.
That is the whole idea.
"Sampling is measuring a continuous signal at regular time intervals, giving a sequence of numbers.
If the signal's highest frequency is below half the sample rate, which is Nyquist, the samples contain all the information.
If not, higher frequencies fold back as aliases: a 900 hertz tone sampled at 1 kilohertz looks like 100 hertz.
So you put an anti-alias low-pass filter ahead of the ADC and sample comfortably faster than twice the bandwidth. Sampling discretizes time; quantization discretizes amplitude."
